en.justification: Probably commissioned by Cardinal Borghese, the Dutch artist, Rubens, is the author of this painting (1606–08) on a biblical theme that was popular during the Counter-Reformation: the fight between truth and virtue (personified by Susanna) and lies (symbolised by the elders).

This German court church is inspired by the Baroque style of northern Italy where many foreign artists worked. Agostino Barelli drew up the initial designs while Enrico Zucalli worked as the construction supervisor. François Cuvilliés the Elder re-designed the façade between 1765 and 1768. All the altarpieces of the church are by Italian masters of the Bolognese and Venetian schools.
The interior has rich stucco decoration by Nicolò Petri (1685–88), and Wolfgang Leutner was responsible for the stucco figures.
The altar paintings are by Caspar de Crayer, Carlo Cignani, George Desmareés and Joachim Sandrart; the statues of the saints Marcus and John are by Balthasar Ableithner.

Born in Croatia in 1667, Benkovich spent most of his adult life abroad in Venice and then in Bologna (1706), where he worked with Carlo Cignani and Giuseppe Maria Crespi. He painted great compositions for Würzburg castle and later worked for Prince Lothar Franz Schönborn in the Weissenstein palace gallery, Pommersfelden, in around 1715.

Danish painter Jacob van Schuppen studied with Nicolas Largilliere. He travelled to Vienna in 1716 where, ten years later, he was instrumental in the revival of the Academy of Fine Arts. Known as a portraitist, van Schuppen’s genre painting can be found in several Hungarian collections.

Domenico Scarlatti (1685–1757) arrived in Portugal in around 1720 having been appointed music teacher to the children of King João V. He then became *Kappelmeister* of the orchestra and choir of the Patriarchal Seminar chapel where he introduced Italian Opera and the new European musical and artistic patterns in vogue at that time. Under the patronage of King João V, from 1729, he lived in Madrid as music master to the king's daughter, Maria Bárbara, who was the wife of the future King Philip VI of Spain.

The ceiling fresco of the Feudal Hall in the Episcopal residence of Kroměříž is by the Austrian artist Franz Anton Maulbertsch, who worked throughout the countries of the Habsburg Empire and was a major influence on his many followers. The residential complex for the bishops consists of a chateau with a lower- and also a floral garden.
Detail of the ceiling fresco.
Detail of the ceiling fresco.
Detail of the ceiling fresco.

Around 1543 the Portuguese (or as they were known, the *Namban-jin*) arrived in Japan, and so began a period of rich cultural exchange. This pair of *byobu*, made by Japanese artists, is a unique visual document of the presence of the *Namban-jin* in Japan. Portuguese traders and the Japanese exemplify the cultural encounters seen in this procession, or *Namban Gyoretsu*, which is passing a Japanese street observed by curious inhabitants.

en.detail_name: A melting pot of cultures: the procession or *Gyoretsu*
en.justification: The procession is composed of a Captain-Major, standing underneath a parasol surrounded by other officers, as well as sailors, African slaves, Indians and Malays. The expensive dresses and ornaments of the aristocrats and merchants are clearly visible. The majority wear *bombacha* – large baggy trousers worn in the East to protect the wearer from mosquitoes – and their doublets have buttons, unknown to the Japanese before the Portuguese arrived, who called them *botan* from the Portuguese *botão.*

en.detail_name: A world in miniature: the great ship from Macao, or *kurofune* (“the black ship”)
en.justification: The transaction of goods on a global scale linked cultures and commercial ambitions. These exotic objects included Chinese folding-chairs, lacquered boxes, porcelain, bundles and bales of silk, and Arabian caged animals. Between the 16th and 17th centuries, Portugal established trade routes along the coastline of the Indian Ocean, the Southern Seas and the China Sea.

Missionaries wait in front of the Jesuit church built in the Japanese style: its interior largely follows local models seen in the use of *tatami* to cover the floor and *shoji* and *fusuma* to divide the inner space. The Japanese paid special attention to the “accommodation” of Portuguese and European missionaries, working hard to integrate foreign settlers into Japanese society, which this scene eloquently details.

The monumental Early Baroque Town Hall designed by Elias Holl, contains the magnificent Goldener Saal or Golden Hall. Augsburg was an affluent city with a population of wealthy merchants, bankers, publishers and practitioners in the applied arts.

en.name: Golden Hall
en.artist: Design, wall paintings and ceiling paintings: Johann Matthias Kager (1575–1634)
en.justification: The Golden Hall, designed as a meeting place for the Reichstag, is adorned with a magnificent ceiling. Surrounding the central image are four oval paintings representing Education, Fertility, Industriousness and Devotion. The valour of Augsburg is also celebrated with the inscription on the banner, which reads: “enemies will be defeated”. Four oval frames surrounding the banner represent the allegorical arts of Healing; Honesty, Justice and Prosperity.

In around 1683, throughout Europe, it was common for large metallic basins with handles to be placed on the ground to cool bottles and ewers during mealtimes. These metal prototypes were then sent to China where potters copied them in porcelain, decorating them according to clients’ taste. This cooler would have been used to store bottles, and with a special mount in place, glasses also. Along with another set, this pair of coolers is unique in shape and decoration among exported Chinese porcelain.

This impressive example of Bavarian *trompe l'oeil* façade fresco, known locally as *Lüftlmalerei*, was executed by Franz Seraph Zwinck. It was commissioned by a wealthy merchant, Anton Lang, who was a well-known collector and dealer in private devotional carvings which were very popular in Bavaria at the time. Lang had trading connections in Spain, Portugal and further afield.

This house with its fine frescoes, and the other houses like it in the region, were status symbols for their residents and for the whole area. The two façades are adorned with biblical scenes that are fully integrated with the *trompe l'oeil*\-enhanced actual doors and windows. This creates the illusion of a much larger house and enhances the viewer's appreciation of the biblical narrative in terms of everyday, concrete reality.
Detail of the fresco painting.

The Portuguese missions spread Christianity among the local Asian populations, preaching to the indigenous peoples, learning the local languages and familiarising themselves with the indigenous cultures. The Jesuit St. João de Brito was sent to the mission in Maduré, India, in 1673 with the aim of converting the higher castes. He became a *pandaraswami*, an Indian ascetic. His execution in Orbyur, India, in 1690 was ordered by the Raja of Marava.
That the reliquary chest was commissioned by King Pedro II of Portugal as a royal homage to the Jesuit saint can be verified by the Portuguese coat-of-arms in the centre.
Jan Neumayer was an artist of the Olomouc workshop who probably trained in Italy. He, together with a counterpart in Šternberk, developed the folk faience tradition.
The Benedictine Abbey at Tihany was founded in 1055 by King András I of the Árpád dynasty (1046–60) in honour of the Virgin Mary and the titular saint Anianus (Aignan).

en.name: The Mariazell altar
en.date: Installed in 1762 (figurine of the Virgin Mary replaced in 1889)
en.location:
Benedictine Abbey of St Aignan in Tihany  
  
Tihany, Veszprém County
en.artist: Altarpiece carver: József Hubert; painter-gilder: József Cordelli
en.justification: The cult of Mariazell arrived in Hungary via the Benedictine abbey in Dömölk and then grew in popularity following nomination of Sámuel Vajda the former administrator of the abbey. The erection of the altar and the establishment of the cult of Mariazell are directly attributed to Vajda’s activities.

The Pilgrimage Church is located in a southern Moravian village that once belonged to the Znojmo-Louka Premonstratensian Monastery. A unique series of buildings and pilgrimage sites associated with the main religious festivals of the liturgical year were built around the monastery.

The miraculous Christ figure was brought by a monk from Louka monastery from the Steingaden Monastery in Bavaria. It was a replica of an adoration statue at the local Wieskirche, but as it was believed to heal the sick and enjoyed enormous respect and veneration, a new church was built on the site of Louka Monastery and the statue was installed on the high altar.

An Early Baroque transformation of a Late Gothic hall-church, designed by Hans Krumpper, to become a complex mix of a pilgrimage and a convent church with stuccowork in the style of the Wessobrunn School. Among the Rococo additions are a fine tabernacle, designed and carved by Johann Baptist Straub, and a reliquary chapel with Neapolitan-inspired ceiling paintings by Johann Baptist Baader.
Reliquary chapel, with Neapolitan-inspired ceiling paintings.

Venerated by the Portuguese, this pilgrimage sanctuary of the type known as *Sacro Monte* (Way of the Cross), includes a large, complex Baroque stairway – along which are chapels, statues and allegorical fountains – leading to the upper square where the Neoclassical-style Bom Jesus Church is located.

A grandiose staircase leads up to the church. It is subdivided into three stairways with terraces dedicated to the five Senses and five Virtues. The stairway of the five Senses conveys individual redemption, promoting a notion that evil becomes good by controlling the instincts (the senses), and through an appreciation of the spirit instead of the physical and carnal desires.

The six fountains – sculpted in granite with *rocaille* details – are located on the central axis of the ensemble, installed against an ornamental Baroque background. Allegorical figures, each representing one of the five Senses, crown the fountains.

The stairway of the five Senses leads up to the Crucifixion Chapel. On the way up are other chapels, one of which, the Chapel of the Flagellation, reinforces the Suffering of Christ or the *Via Crucis* as an element of purification.

A Late Gothic church building with stucco decoration in the Late Regency style. It holds altars from a number of eras of the Baroque, among which are the well-known Altar of the Conception and the oval Sanctuary Chapel.
The Altar of the Conception has a painting donated by the Munich court painter, Peter Candid.

John of Nepomuk was a major Moravian saint at the turn of the 17th century. After tbe Czech martyr was murdered in 1393 his cult spread all over the Czech territories and throughout Roman Catholic Europe, even spreading overseas. The saint was worshipped even before his canonisation and beatification in Rome in 1729.

In Coimbra University library the *chinoiserie* motifs on the bookshelves entice the visitor with a taste of exoticism while the allegorical ceiling paintings recall the globalised world built under the Portuguese. On the wall facing the door is a portrait of King João V by the court painter G. D. Duprà.

The bookshelves, containing around 60,000 books, are lacquered in various colours in each room; green, red and black, and decorated with *chinoiserie* motifs. They are all two-storeys high, with a balcony and the stairs embedded within the fixed furniture.
Example of *chinoiserie* motifs.

The Esterházy palace complex is a *maison de' plaisance* that was redesigned by Nikolaus Esterházy between 1750 and 1780. The palace was the centre of Hungarian *chinoiserie*, and the opera house and marionette theatre were exquisite parts of the complex. Franz Joseph Haydn was head of Prince Nikolaus’s orchestra for 30 years and lived at the palace.

In the 18th century the palace was famous for its exquisite furnishings, including silk tapestries, ornate *boiserie* panels and wall-paintings; chandeliers, clocks, ceramics, books, carpets, furniture and paintings; [*chinoiserie*](javascript:showGlossary\('chinoiserie','en'\);), including furniture, ceramics and also [blue-and-white](javascript:showGlossary\('blue-and-white','en'\);) wall-paintings, wallpaper and Chinese lacquered panels.
Japanese ceramics.
Japanese ceramics.
Chinese-lacquer panels.

The single nave has two overlapping choirs separated from the church by an oval frame. The decorative scheme includes *azulejos* and oil paintings from the late 17th and early 18th centuries and a Rococo main altarpiece. The convent includes the southern and northern cloisters, dating from the 16th century and the 17th century respectively.
The Upper Choir has an oratory, an 18th-century organ and choir-stalls and *chinoiserie* decoration on the arch-vault that opens into the church.
*Chinoiserie* elements on the arch-vault of the upper choir.
*Chinoiserie* elements on the arch.

Count Questenberk travelled around western Europe and planned to model his residence on the palace at Versailles. Its Baroque reconstruction was by the Austrian architect, J. Prandtauer, and included a garden in the French style. In the 18th century the château functioned as a centre for high culture with a large library, a gallery, a theatre and a musical ensemble.
The *salla terrena* is decorated with illusory ornamental paintings evoking an overgrown pergola, while Japanese genre scenes decorate the adjoining lounge.

The “Chinese” room, which was adjoined to the library, had a floor composed of several different kinds of wood by the court joiner. The count consulted with an adviser from Vienna, Conrad Adolph von Albrecht, who also worked for the Sinzendorfs in Židlochovice.

en.name: Ambassadors’ Room
en.artist: Carver: Jacques Antoine Colin; Woodworker: Jean-François Cragnier; Painters: Bruno José do Vale and Francisco de Melo
en.justification: The Palace of Queluz was a project undertaken by Infante Dom Pedro (later King Pedro III, 1717–86) from 1747 until 1786 to transform his former summer manor into a Royal Palace. In the “Room of Vases” are enormous Chinese porcelain vases and smaller, similarly Oriental vessels. The ceiling paintings and the ogee arches hold allegorical motifs and *chinoiserie*.

en.name: Corridor of Sleeves
en.artist: Ceramist and painter: Francisco Jorge da Costa
en.justification: The polychrome tile-panels covering the upper walls depict the Four Seasons, the Four Continents and scenes from classical mythology, with *singerie*s and *chinoiserie* with figures in Oriental costumes.

en.name: Tile Canal of the Jamor river
en.artist: Azulejos by João Antunes and Manuel da Costa Rosado
en.justification: The canal, decorated with *azulejos* panels, was originally located close to the “Chinese House” decorated in *chinoiserie*. The Queen’s chamber orchestra would have played on summer evenings inside or outside the house while the royal family drifted in boats on the mirrored waters of the canal, lit by torches, and reflecting the *azulejos*.

en.name: Oriental influence on the royal collections
en.artist: Made by Chinese artisans; design by Cornelius Pronk (1691–1759)
en.justification: These Fountain and Basin from the Qing dynasty depict narrative scenes are named *The Doctor's Visit to the Emperor*, by a drawing of Cornelius Pronk (1691–1759). Hired by the Ducht East India Company he painted imaginary scenes from China, where he never went, to be furtherly copied by oriental artisans to whom a large scale of dinner sets was ordered for the European market.

The vase, produced in Delft, belonged to countess Jelisava Drašković. The shape and painted plant ornamentation in blue, red-brown and green is of Oriental inspiration. It is signed in red-brown: “APK” (in ligature) and engraved “X”.

Illustrating the book by Lorenzo Legati (Bologna, 1677), the etching shows the interior of Marquis Ferdinando Cospi’s museum. Cospi’s collection grew due to his contacts and exchanges with travellers and correspondents abroad. The marquis is a good example of 17th-century encyclopaedic taste, which for him, appears to be inspired more by curiosity and wonder than by a true scientific interest.
Façade of a late medieval citizen’s house with rich stucco decoration executed by Anton Gigl from the Bavarian Wessobrunn School.
Detail of the façade.

Church with a nave and eight side chapels. The interior decoration of the Chapel of St. John the Baptist was commissioned from Rome in 1740 by King João V (1706–50). All the elements arrived, dismantled, in Lisbon by boat having been blessed in Rome. Construction took place between 1742 and 1750, the year when it was officially inaugurated.

The chapel, in the Roman Baroque style, has ornamented surfaces in coloured marble and several other types of ornamental stone. All the objects for the Chapel of St. John the Baptist were made in Rome by Italian artists. The collection of liturgical objects was produced at the same time as the interior decoration (1743 and 1749): gold-embroidered vestments, several metal objects – candleholders, reliquaries and crucifixes – and also books for the Mass.

A splendid pair of torch holders in gilt bronze and chiselled silver which are part of the royal commission for the Chapel of St. John the Baptist. All the objects for the chapel were designed and produced in Rome by Italian artists headed by Giuseppe Gagliardi, with assistants Fellice Schiffone, Agostino Ancidoni, Lucano Celladini, and Luciano Morelli.

The architect Enrico Zuccalli (c. 1642–8 to March 1724) was born in Switzerland and worked in Bavaria and Cologne. Living in Munich after 1669 until his death, he was responsible for the introduction of Italian Baroque architecture to Germany. Among his works is Lustheim Palace, the summer residence of the politically ambitious prince-elector Maximilian I Emanuel, with splendid interiors and a picture gallery. Designed in the style of an Italian villa, Lustheim has a central rectangular ballroom, side-wings with residential rooms and a belvedere above the central wing.

en.name: Ceiling fresco of the Great Hall
en.location: New Castle, second floor of the middle section
en.justification: At one time this was the world’s largest ceiling fresco, depicting the fight between Aeneas and Turnus for the hand of the king’s daughter, Lavinia. Maximilian II Emanuel is sometimes recognised in the facial features of Aeneas.

The Church is decorated with Baroque oil paintings and *azulejos* depicting religious scenes, carved gilt-wood altarpieces and sculptures. From 1698 to 1707 Dutch tile-painters, along with the Spanish master Gabriel del Barco, made the *azulejos* seen in the nave and main chapel. The early 16th-century Convent of Madre Deus (1509 and 1517) founded by Queen Leonor (1458–1525), was expanded, together with the church, gradually, mainly during the Baroque era.

en.name: Dutch tiles of the main chapel
en.location:
Main Chapel, Church and Convent of Madre de Deus  
  
Lisbon
en.justification: The *azulejos* in the main chapel are by Jan van Oort, depicting the vision of Pope Nicholas V when standing by the body of St. Francis.

en.name: Dutch tiles, Portuguese paintings and rocaille gilded wood pulpit
en.location:
Nave, Church and Convent of Madre de Deus  
  
Lisbon
en.artist: Willem van der Kloet [n.d.]; Bento Coelho da Silveira (1648–1708)
en.justification: The *azulejos* in the nave was commissioned in Holland and is by the Dutch artist Willem van der Kloet. Close to the *rocaille* pulpit are *azulejos* featuring Franciscan monks praying. The walls, adorned with paintings by Bento Coelho da Silveira, depict the Life of St. Claire and the Life of St. Francis.

en.name: Triumphal arch paintings
en.location: Nave and main chapel, Church and Convent of Madre de Deus
en.justification: André Gonçalves was a Portuguese artist who worked in Lisbon with the Genovese painter Giulio Cesar di Teminé. His paintings, which decorate the triumphal arch, feature the Coronation of the Virgin by the Holy Trinity. Other paintings of St. Claire and St. Francis flank the archway.

The monastery complex has works by several prominent artists: in the Chapel of St. Anastasia are the altarpiece painting by the Venetian painter Jacopo Amigoni and a ceiling fresco by the Tyrolean painter Johann Jakob Zeiller. In the Ceremony Hall are ceiling paintings by Stephan and Michael Kessler.

en.name: Benedict Altar (Altar of the abbey church)
en.date: 1686: altar table, altarpiece and niche sculptures; 1696: tabernacle; 1788: altar painting; 1790
en.artist: Altar architecture: Johann Georg Guggemos (1636–1703); niche sculptures and angel: Balthasar Ableithner (1614–1705); Franz Edmund Doll (1744–1824); altar painting: Martin Knoller (1725–1804)
en.justification: Painting of the high altar by the Italian- and Viennese-trained Martin Knoller.

en.name: Anastasia chapel
en.location: North side chancel and sacristy of the abbey church
en.artist: Architecture: Johann Michael Fischer (1692–1766); stuccowork and high altar: Johann Michael Feichtmayr (1696–1772); altar paintings of Anastasia and Immaculata altars: Jacopo Amigoni (1682–1752); frescoes: Johann Jakob Zeiller (1710–1783)
en.justification: Venetian altarpieces in the chapel.

en.name: Tyrolean fresco
en.justification: Tyrolean fresco by a Viennese-trained painter.

Mughal Emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605) was interested in Portuguese Christianity and art. Requesting the authorities in Goa to send a Jesuit mission to his court, it was from this initial contact that a refined artistic style emerged, seen not only in painting, but also in textiles, metalwork, clothing and furniture, such as this cabinet.

The style of the cabinet is based on a Portuguese prototype but the decoration and the materials are from local sources. The doors are decorated with the Tree of Life, a symbol of the Divine for both Christians and Muslims. Among the branches are mythical birds and elephants, while on the lower register, Portuguese figures hunt on horseback with long lances.

A porcelain bottle with the coat-of-arms of King Philip II of Spain, it was inspired both in shape and decoration by a pilgrim’s flask. Flasks such as these were precious objects among 16th-century pilgrims who used them to hold drinking water when on pilgrimage. The shape, which is rare in China, is probably based on a metal model from western Asia.

The church was donated and designed by the erudite and well-travelled medic Hippolytus Guarinoni. The interior, renovated in the 1750s, is famous for its classicising ceiling frescoes by Martin Knoller who trained in Italy.
The frescoes are among the most important achievements of Martin Knoller. The Apotheosis of the church patron in the main dome is surrounded by scenes from the lives of the saints.

The portrait was made during Maxmilián Oldřich Kounic’s Grand Tour to the Haag and Brussels. Kounic, who later became Moravia’s provincial governor, was responsible for selecting the artists to decorate the Assembly Hall of the provincial estates in Brno. He played a major role in the reconstruction of the Kounic family residence in Slavkov, the design of which was one of the first examples of the French-chateau plan in Moravia.

A cycle of seven paintings that exemplify the 18th-century Italian (also French and English) taste for travel, archaeology and antiquities, perspective and landscape. Both artists worked for Pompeo Aldrovandi (1668–1752), a famous Bolognese cardinal who transformed his family home into a sumptuous residence that was inspired by the most famous French models.
From the cycle of seven views with ruins: Archaeology.
From the cycle of seven views with ruins: Perspective.
From the cycle of seven views with ruins: Landscape.

This bourgeois Rococo palace was designed by Karl Albert Lespilliez for Benedikt Adam Liebert von Liebenhofen (1713–1818), a banker and international trader in silver. The palace is best known for its richly decorated ballroom with ceiling frescoes by the Venetian painter Gregorio Guglielmi.

en.name: Ballroom
en.artist: Design and ceiling frescoes: Gregorio Guglielmi (1714–1773); stuccowork: Franz-Xaver Feichtmayr (1735–1803), Simpert Feichtmayr (1732–1806); carving: Placidus Verhelst (1727–78)
en.justification: The long ballroom (measuring 23 m x11 m) is exquisitely decorated with carved ornamentation and elaborate stuccowork, walls adorned with ornamentally framed panels by Placidius Verhelst, and a number of ornate mirrors. The *sopraporte* or overdoor paintings and the ceiling fresco are by Gregorio Gugliemi.

The Portuguese (*namban jin*) arrived in Japan in 1543. The Portuguese black ships (*kurofune*) arrived in Japan laden with exotic cargo, people – including missionaries – treasures and novelties. All this is depicted in masterly detail: on the right is a Jesuit church and residence, where, outside waiting prominently depicted, are missionaries.

Missionaries are waiting in front of the church. The Jesuits were responsible for the Portuguese presence in Japan and based their religious work at a cultural level. They became the European focal point in Japan, interacting with the political elite, the Buddhist temples and some of the population.

Having just arrived at a Japanese port, a group surveys the unloading of a precious cargo. The core business at this time was the trade of Chinese silk for Japanese silver, which was then sold in China for fabulous profits. Nearby, a heterogeneous procession is being led by the ship’s captain who is shielded by an umbrella. Portuguese gentleman and merchants, Arabians, Indians, Africans and Malays are also part of the procession.

The lacquered *Namban* oratory with doors embellished with mother-of-pearl inlay in a floral design both inside and out, holds a painting of the Virgin Mary with the infant Jesus in her arms. On the triangular pediment that surmounts it there is a monogram *IHS* (the abbreviation of the Greek *IHSOUS*, or JESUS). The oratory is an example of the possible interaction between the Jesuit painting school – operating in Japan since the 1580s – and the Japanese pupils who quickly demonstrated skill in Western-style painting.
Floral design in gold and silver powder (*maki-e*) and mother-of-pearl inlay (*raden*).

The Sala Regia was the venue for important meetings between the Pope and ambassadors or with foreign delegations from Japan, Congo, Persia, Armenia and Ethiopia. The frieze refers to Eastern legations that visited Rome at the beginning of the 17th century, the relationship between Europe and the East and the missionary activity promoted by Pope Paul V.
Japanese Hasekura Tsunenaga’s visit to Rome in 1615.
Two Persian ambassadors’ visit to Rome in 1609.

Depictions of the Congolese delegation sent in 1608 and the visit of the Armenian Patriarch in 1610, or possibly a depiction of the representatives sent by the Ethiopian Negus Sultan Sagued in that same year.

Ivan III (1640–83) had been a page at the court of Emperor Leopold I. In 1678 he departed for Mexico, landing in Vera Cruz two years later where he lived among the Tarahumara Indians as a missionary. He wrote about his travels in Latin, documenting his journey to Mexico and New Mexico, which he enriched with a map of Tarahumara which plots missionary settlements and Spanish fortresses.

Surrounding the central oval portrait are four scenes from Ivan III’s life as a Jesuit and a family coat-of-arms, all enclosed within separate painted frames. The artist is unknown, but the portrait dates to the first decades of the 18th century.

Surrounding the central oval portrait are four scenes from Ivan III’s life as a Jesuit and a family coat-of-arms, all enclosed within separate painted frames. The artist is unknown, but the portrait dates to the first decades of the 18th century.

Surrounding the central oval portrait are four scenes from Ivan III’s life as a Jesuit and a family coat-of-arms, all enclosed within separate painted frames. The artist is unknown, but the portrait dates to the first decades of the 18th century.

A large commode/oratory with a desk and drawers that was designed for use onboard ship. This portable piece of furniture, which was used either for religious purposes or as a cabinet-on-a-stand with a desk and storage, was the result of commercial exchanges among merchants who travelled via existing Portuguese trade routes to overseas colonies and ports or to north or north-western Europe. Several artistic styles may have influenced its design: the highly valued screens and furniture from Coromandel (on the southeastern coast of the Indian Subcontinent), Chinese folding screens (*Henan*), or English Japanned furniture.
Painted in vibrant red lacquer, it has black decorative tablets and gilded iconographic motifs or *chinoiserie*s.
Inside the cupboard there is an oratory embellished with religious scenes; the inside surface of the doors are painted with scenes from the Passion of Christ.

Containing a portable altar, the chest was designed to be transported long distances on Portuguese maritime voyages, and enabled seafarers to celebrate Mass both while onboard ship and on arrival in foreign lands. Portable altars of this sort were lightweight and easy to move and store, thus they met the need to reduce the volume and weight onboard ships. During voyages, priests were obliged to celebrate Mass every Sunday and on holy days. A particular feature of a Mass celebrated onboard ship was that there was no communion as ships were not consecrated, thus it is known as  “dry Mass”. Altars in the houses of Portuguese settlers were commonplace, normally set up in the largest room so that a congregational Mass could be held.
The liturgical implements necessary to celebrate Mass were stored in a drawer below the altar table in customised, made-to-measure indentations.

Mass could only be celebrated on altars that contained an altar-stone that had been blessed and upon which were placed the chalice and the host. In this altar, the altar-stone is found in a concave indentation within the table.
A central altar card from a set of three, which were kept as a memory aid for the celebrant of the Mass.

Lisbon is recorded on this tile panel, measuring almost 23 m-wide, produced before the earthquake of 1755. Depicting approximately 14 km of the riverbank, it shows a vast panoramic view of the capital and its outskirts, with focus  on the centre of political and economic power, including the development of the city around the Royal Palace of Ribeira. Lisbon played a major role in the dissemination throughout Europe of new products, tastes and habits.

Built by King Manuel I in the 16th century close to the River Tagus, the royal palace was totally destroyed by the earthquake in 1755. The palace was a scenic setting for the court and an impressive venue for receiving diplomats: the Terreiro do Paço or court terrace was the main setting or point of departure for bullfights, the *auto-de-fé* of the Inquisition, Corpus Christi festivities and promenades on the river.

The painted miniature depicts King João V of Portugal seated and surrounded by a group of courtesans who are being served coffee and chocolate. These beverages, which at first were very fashionable among Portuguese aristocracy, then became popular throughout the rest of Europe. Set within an ornate silver frame displaying the royal coat-of-arms, this is one of only a few Joanine court artefacts to have survived the Earthquake of 1755.
A coffee pot, hot chocolate maker, tea cups and a bottle alluding to the popularity of these beverages among the elite.

While the design for this type of furniture is typical of Venetian production, its purpose reflects the contemporary European enthusiasm for the art of the Far East, especially porcelain and lacquerwork. Although lacquer and porcelain objects were imported into Europe, European craftsmen attempted to master the techniques of lacquer and porcelain production. The first European porcelain factories opened in the first-half of the 18th century. The popularity of these wares resulted in special porcelain- and lacquerwork display halls in mansions and palaces, and the use of bureau cabinets such as this one.
Shelves displaying porcelain ware.

The Hungarian painter, Jacob Bogdány, travelled throughout Vienna and Amsterdam and finally reached  London in 1688, where he worked for the English royal family. He painted animal compositions, mainly exotic birds, designed to go above doors or for mantelpieces.

For this picture Minderhout works in the tradition of morality scenes based on aristocratic society. It was probably inspired by the prints of Claude Gillot (1673–1722) featuring scenes from *commedia dell´arte*, and the work of Hendrick Govaerts (1669–1720), from Antwerp, who was active in Prague and Vienna during the period when theatre established itself as part of court life. This type of scene was influenced by the Galli-Bibiena family, who were decorators to the Vienna court and well-known for their theatre designs, and whose members and pupils worked for the Czech and Moravian nobility. Czech and Moravian aristocrats often attended performances in Vienna and cultivated theatre culture in their own palaces.
Figures wearing exotic costumes.

A gilded-silver and gold monstrance encrusted with precious jewels and distingued by quality chiselling, which is the result of Portugal’s trade with Brazil. Scholars attribute it to J. F. Ludovice, the German goldsmith and architect of the convent of Mafra. The sunburst, encircled by clouds, has irregular rays that are encrusted with precious stones.

The surface of the monstrance is encrusted with precious stones mined in Brazil, some of them large, and all of them excellent quality. The spectacular decorative and chromatic effect created by the metal and gemstones befits the Baroque sense of theatre.

This church was dedicated to the founder of the Jesuits and was commissioned by Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi in 1626. The vault, which is one of the the world’s largest, represents the saints Ignacio Loyola, Francis Xavier, Luís Gonzaga and Francesco Borgia, all of whom were canonised or beatified during the first two decades of the 17th century.

St. Ignatius of Loyola was the main founder and the first Superior General of the Society of Jesus, a religious order professing a vow of obedience directly to the Pope in so far as missionary duties were concerned. The early Jesuits were sent by Ignatius to pagan lands where they worked on the propagation and strengthening of the Catholic faith.
Chained and defeated by the evangelising mission of the Jesuits are personifications of Vice and Error.

This painting, part of a set of 20 and probably by André Reinoso, was commissioned by the Jesuits for the sacristy of the Church of St. Roque. The scene features the ardent preaching of St. Frances Xavier in the cosmopolitan city of Goa shortly after his arrival there in 1542. It is particularly interesting from the ethnographic point of view in that it illustrates a variety of oriental customs as well as different social classes.
A crowd of new converts includes men, women and children as well Portuguese noblemen on horseback, all of whom surround the saint.
The portrait of St. Francis Xavier is one of only a few easel paintings by Andrea Pozzo. It was brought to Požega by the Jesuits soon after 1698 following liberation from the Ottomans.
A Jesuit church that paraphrases Salzburg Cathedral, it was executed and decorated with Early Baroque geometrical stuccowork in the style of the Munich court by the Bavarian Wessobrunn school.

Altarpieces in the St. Francis Xavier side-chapel glorify St. Ignatius and St. Francis both of whom were canonised in 1622. The altarpiece shown here, located on the back wall of the chapel, depicts St. Ignatius baptising an Indian nobleman.

The other painting recounts a scene from the miracles of St. Frances Xavier when a sea-crab returned a small crucifix the missionary had lost at sea. Both representations refer to the Jesuits’ role within the context of their Counter-Reformation missionary work.

Established in 1578, construction of the complex was sponsored by Cardinal and Count František of Dietrichstein, the prime mover of the re-Catholicisation of Moravia, and his brother, Provincial Vice-Chamberlain Zikmund. The college ceased to exist with the dissolution of the Jesuit order in 1773.
The monumental altar (1734–37) over a silver tabernacle, holds a replica painting of the Virgin Mary from the largest Marian church, Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome.
The figure of an adoring Blackamoor complements the iconography of the altar.

Father António Vieira, a Portuguese Jesuit Priest, writer and preacher was born in Lisbon in 1608. As a senior diplomat and missionary in Brazil he became both an influential figure in Portuguese culture and a principle leader in the defense of human rights both among Brazil’s indigenous peoples and among Jews persecuted by the Inquisition. Acquainted with the languages and costumes of the Brazilian Indians, he was a missionary and a preacher with a humanistic vision and played a key role in building the relationships between Jesuits, the colonisers and indigenous peoples.

After independence from Spanish domination Vieira returned to Lisbon where he proposed some economic reforms entailing the end of the Inquisition’s distinction between new and old Christians in order to attract the investment of Jews who had fled the kingdom. The idea generated a conflict with the Society of Jesus and the Inquisition.
